#396. How to Tell If It’s a Cyberattack or Just an Outage

Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screwup grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.

The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.

“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”

So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.

The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.

As the head of internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One's default position should be that it isn't a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”

Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”

In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.

In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.

On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.

It can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech company may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.

Another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with issues. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products, Google Workspace, telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.

When a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying issue. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon—but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net. Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his social media accounts.

When IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng says. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy update, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.

Even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what's actually going on,” she says.

Most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.

Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. In other cases, like the NotPetya or WannaCry worms—two of the worst cyberattacks in history—the hackers’ self-perpetuating code left behind ransom messages on machines that quickly spread on social media as the attacks unfolded. Ideological “hacktivist” groups—or state-sponsored hackers working for military or intelligence agencies but posing as hacktivists—also often take credit for their cyberattacks on platforms like X, Telegram, or their own websites. These messages then quickly spread to social media and through news reports.

Even these statements, however, should be taken as just another significant data point: Hacker groups exaggerate, misdirect, or lie when it serves their purposes. And some significant mass hacking incidents—such as the Mirai attack on the internet infrastructure company Dyn in 2016 that took down thousands of websites—have been accompanied by no public message at all from the hackers responsible.

In cases where neither the perpetrator of a hacking incident nor its target has confirmed the attack, confirmation can sometimes come first from a government agency—such as the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency—or even from threat intelligence researchers at private cybersecurity firms. Government and industry investigators sometimes post their findings to their websites or share them with media, but it often takes days, weeks, or even months to come to confirmed conclusions. Hence, step five.

If all these other measures of determining the cause of an outage don’t offer a clear understanding of the situation, the best approach may be patience. “It's going to get a little conclusive at some point,” Madory says. “Sometimes you just have to just sit and wait.”

Aside from the time it takes for companies to admit to their screwups—or hackers to claim a win—the length of an outage can also sometimes offer a clue to its cause. A faulty update, power outage, or cascading bug can often be resolved quickly. Determined hackers who have maximized their damage, who shift tactics to outsmart defenders, or who may still be in a network they’ve breached can cause far longer and more severe outages. “A rollback takes minutes or hours,” Tomé says, referring to reverting to older code as a fix for a faulty update that introduces a bug. “Ransomware takes days or sometimes even weeks.”

In other words, as with all breaking news, when facts are in short supply, it’s better to maintain skepticism about early rumors or conspiracy theories and wait for more concrete evidence.

In the information vacuum that precedes that evidence, it can be easy to see connections between events that may just be coincidences. What are the odds, you may ask, that five major IT outages occurred on a sequential Thursday, Friday, Monday, and Tuesday?

For Doug Madory, who tracks those network outages every day of the week, that string of failures may just be a sign of the increasing complexity of technology—and how fundamentally our civilization has come to depend on it. “For better or worse, modern society is completely mediated through internet-based services. They have outages from time to time. And that’s a reality I don't think we’ll ever completely eliminate,” Madory says.

“If you're immersed in that world of looking at outages for years on end, then they don't really surprise you,” he adds. “You just try to understand what's different about each one. And maybe what we can learn from it.”

#393. The haunting Masters meltdown that changed Rory McIlroy's career

Editor’s Note:  This story was originally published in April 2023.

Slumped on his club, head buried in his arm, Rory McIlroy looked on the verge of tears.

The then-21-year-old had just watched his ball sink into the waters of Rae’s Creek at Augusta National and with it, his dream of winning The Masters, a dream that had looked so tantalizingly close mere hours earlier.

As a four-time major winner and one of the most decorated names in the sport’s history, few players would turn down the chance to swap places with McIlroy heading into Augusta this week.

Yet on Sunday afternoon of April 10, 2011, not a golfer in the world would have wished to be in the Northern Irishman’s shoes.

A fresh-faced, mop-headed McIlroy had touched down in Georgia for the first major of the season with a reputation as the leading light of the next generation of stars.

An excellent 2010 had marked his best season since turning pro three years earlier, highlighted by a first PGA Tour win at the Quail Hollow Championship and a crucial contribution to Team Europe’s triumph at the Ryder Cup.

Yet despite a pair of impressive top-three finishes at the Open and PGA Championship respectively, a disappointing missed cut at The Masters – his first at a major – served as ominous foreshadowing.

McIlroy shot 74 and 77 to fall four strokes short of the cut line at seven-over par, a performance that concerned him enough to take a brief sabbatical from competition.

But one year on in 2011, any lingering Masters demons looked to have been exorcised as McIlroy flew round the Augusta fairways.

Having opened with a bogey-free seven-under 65 – the first time he had ever shot in the 60s at the major – McIlroy pulled ahead from Spanish first round co-leader Alvaro Quirós with a second round 69.

It sent him into the weekend holding a two-shot cushion over Australia’s Jason Day, with Tiger Woods a further stroke behind and back in the hunt for a 15th major after a surging second round 66.

And yet the 21-year-old leader looked perfectly at ease with having a target on his back. Even after a tentative start to the third round, McIlroy rallied with three birdies across the closing six holes to stretch his lead to four strokes heading into Sunday.

The youngster was out on his own ahead of a bunched chasing pack comprising Day, Ángel Cabrera, K.J. Choi and Charl Schwartzel. After 54 holes, McIlroy had shot just three bogeys.

“It’s a great position to be in … I’m finally feeling comfortable on this golf course,” McIlroy told reporters.

“I’m not getting ahead of myself, I know how leads can dwindle away very quickly. I have to go out there, not take anything for granted and go out and play as hard as I’ve played the last three days. If I can do that, hopefully things will go my way.

“We’ll see what happens tomorrow because four shots on this golf course isn’t that much.”

The truth can hurt, and McIlroy was about to prove his assessment of Augusta to be true in the most excruciating way imaginable.

His fourth bogey of the week arrived immediately. Having admitted to expecting some nerves at the first tee, McIlroy sparked a booming opening drive down the fairway, only to miss his putt from five feet.

Three consecutive pars steadied the ship, but Schwartzel had the wind in his sails. A blistering birdie, par, eagle start had seen him draw level at the summit after his third hole.

A subsequent bogey from the South African slowed his charge, as McIlroy clung onto a one-shot lead at the turn from Schwartzel, Cabrera, Choi, and a rampaging Woods, who shot five birdies and an eagle across the front nine to send Augusta into a frenzy.

Despite his dwindling advantage and the raucous Tiger-mania din ahead of him, McIlroy had responded well to another bogey at the 5th hole, draining a brilliant 20-foot putt at the 7th to restore his lead.

The fist pump that followed marked the high-water point of McIlroy’s round, as a sliding start accelerated into full-blown free-fall at the par-four 10th hole.

His tee shot went careening into a tree, ricocheting to settle between the white cabins that separate the main course from the adjacent par-three course. It offered viewers a glimpse at a part of Augusta rarely seen on broadcast, followed by pictures of McIlroy anxiously peering out from behind a tree to track his follow-up shot.

Though his initial escape was successful, yet another collision with a tree and a two-putt on the green saw a stunned McIlroy eventually tap in for a triple bogey. Having led the field one hole and seven shots earlier, he arrived at the 11th tee in seventh.

By the time his tee drive at the 13th plopped into the creek, all thoughts of who might be the recipient of the green jacket had long-since switched away from the anguished youngster. It had taken him seven putts to navigate the previous two greens, as a bogey and a double bogey dropped him to five-under – the score he had held after just 11 holes of the tournament.

Mercifully, the last five holes passed without major incident. A missed putt for birdie from five feet at the final hole summed up McIlroy’s day, though he was given a rousing reception as he left the green.

Mere minutes earlier, the same crowd had erupted as Schwartzel sunk his fourth consecutive birdie to seal his first major title. After starting the day four shots adrift of McIlroy, the South African finished 10 shots ahead of him, and two ahead of second-placed Australian duo Jason Day and Adam Scott.

McIlroy’s eight-over 80 marked the highest score of the round. Having headlined the leaderboard for most of the week, he finished tied-15th.

Tears would flow during a phone call with his parents the following morning, but at his press conference, McIlroy was upbeat.

“I’m very disappointed at the minute, and I’m sure I will be for the next few days, but I’ll get over it,” he said.

“I was leading this golf tournament with nine holes to go, and I just unraveled … It’s a Sunday at a major, what it can do.

“This is my first experience at it, and hopefully the next time I’m in this position I’ll be able to handle it a little better. I didn’t handle it particularly well today obviously, but it was a character-building day … I’ll come out stronger for it.”

Once again, McIlroy would be proven right.

Just eight weeks later in June, McIlroy rampaged to an eight-shot victory at the US Open. Records tumbled in his wake at Congressional, as he shot a tournament record 16-under 268 to become the youngest major winner since Tiger Woods at The Masters in 1997.

The historic victory kickstarted a golden era for McIlroy. After coasting to another eight-shot win at the PGA Championship in 2012, McIlroy became only the third golfer since 1934 to win three majors by the age of 25 with triumph at the 2014 Open Championship.

Before the year was out, he would add his fourth major title with another PGA Championship win.

And much of it was owed to that fateful afternoon at Augusta. In an interview with the BBC in 2015, McIlroy dubbed it “the most important day” of his career.

“If I had not had the whole unravelling, if I had just made a couple of bogeys coming down the stretch and lost by one, I would not have learned as much.

“Luckily, it did not take me long to get into a position like that again when I was leading a major and I was able to get over the line quite comfortably. It was a huge learning curve for me and I needed it, and thankfully I have been able to move on to bigger and better things.

“Looking back on what happened in 2011, it doesn’t seem as bad when you have four majors on your mantelpiece.”

McIlroy’s contentment came with a caveat: it would be “unthinkable” if he did not win The Masters in his career.

Yet as he prepares for his 15th appearance at Augusta National this week, a green jacket remains an elusive missing item from his wardrobe.

Despite seven top-10 finishes in his past 10 Masters outings, the trophy remains the only thing separating McIlroy from joining the ranks of golf immortals to have completed golf’s career grand slam of all four majors in the modern era: Gene Sarazen, Ben Hogan, Gary Player, Jack Nicklaus, and Tiger Woods.

A runner-up finish to Scottie Scheffler last year marked McIlroy’s best finish at Augusta, yet arguably 2011 remains the closest he has ever been to victory. A slow start in 2022 meant McIlroy had begun Sunday’s deciding round 10 shots adrift of the American, who teed off for his final hole with a five-shot lead despite McIlroy’s brilliant 64 finish.

At 33 years old, time is still on his side. Though 2022 extended his major drought to eight years, it featured arguably his best golf since that golden season in 2014.

And as McIlroy knows better than most, things can change quickly at Augusta National.

#391. Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it

While we’re used to predictable technology, AI challenges that assumption. Therefore, the goal must be bounded, observable, and controllable AI.

In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors.

For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses.

AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built.

We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence.

Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside.

Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox.

With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned.

Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event.

It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest.

Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark.

The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do.

Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions:

The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. Invention earns attention. Trust earns adoption.

#389. Nvidia’s Board Has No Plans to Bring Back Jensen Huang

As Nvidia reported its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, the company’s financial performance was overshadowed by the drama surrounding its former CEO. And Nvidia’s board made one thing clear right off the bat: Jensen Huang isn’t coming back.

At the start of the earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones emphasized the company’s strength and “groundbreaking technology” before turning to the circumstances surrounding Huang’s departure.

“On November 12, our board of directors announced that, after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions … and the board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said.

Asked about the company’s strategy for retaining talent and navigating the leadership transition, interim CEO Colette Kress emphasized the importance of the company’s workforce. “Our employees are absolutely instrumental to everything in this company,” Kress said. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure that they are safe and that the work can be done in the current environment.”

Jones added that the Nvidia board is taking the search for a new CEO “very seriously” and is considering both internal and external candidates. National security dynamics are changing the chip industry, Jones said, and “our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully. So the search will be thorough. We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.”

One recurring theme that emerged from the earnings call, aside from the Huang saga: Demand for Nvidia’s chips remains as strong as ever. Kress said that Nvidia expects that it will keep growing throughout 2027 and into 2028, fueled by the rise of agentic AI.

Less than a week after Huang resigned as chief executive, Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the quarter that ended on October 25, 2026. That exceeded analysts’ expectations of roughly $109 billion and was nearly double the revenue reported in the same quarter a year ago.

The vast majority of Nvidia’s revenue came from its data center business, which generated $107.6 billion, up 110 percent from a year ago.

Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, who had served as an executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider called Megaspeed. Then, reports emerged that Nvidia’s longtime leader additionally had an affair with one of his direct reports; following Huang’s resignation, Reuters reported he had an affair with a second employee.

Huang’s relationship with the alleged Chinese operative has raised questions about what he knew about Nvidia’s advanced chips making their way into China despite US export restrictions. Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list in June 2025, but The New York Times reported that, according to third-party data, a subsidiary of Megaspeed “received shipments of more than $800 million of export-controlled Nvidia A.I. technology, including Blackwell and H200 chips,” which were subject to export restrictions.

On the heels of Tuesday’s earnings, Nvidia’s stock rose in after-hours trading. The company had lost more than $1 trillion in market value over the past month amid the fallout from Huang’s scandal.

Earlier on Tuesday, Huang released his first statement since his resignation.

Huang thanked allies for their support, writing he’d “seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.” He admitted to failing to “live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA,” adding he was “committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.”

However, Huang concluded, if the board “decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

Nvidia, which is headquartered in Santa Clara, California, has roughly 60,000 employees, and sentiments have varied in the wake of Huang’s departure. “In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” an employee told WIRED last week.

But in his 33 years leading Nvidia, Huang earned a loyal army of supporters by minimizing layoffs and red tape. Some employees have been calling for his return to the helm. And a few tech industry heavyweights are similarly eager for Huang to be reinstated. Executives including Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan took to X to voice support for Huang, signing a petition to “Bring Jensen Back.”

Huang’s activities are currently under investigation by at least four different entities: the FBI and the US Department of Justice, Congress, the US Securities and Exchange Commission, and an independent law firm appointed by Nvidia’s board. Industry sources previously told WIRED that Huang is unlikely to return to the company any time soon.

Interim CEO Kress, at the end of Tuesday’s call, offered what sounded like a rallying cry for anyone doubting Nvidia’s future without Huang.

“Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed,” Kress said. “We’ve got this.”

#388. The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back

Supporters are signing a petition to reinstate Huang. But findings on Nvidia chips in China and a new Commerce rule are threatening open-source AI’s reputation and progress regardless.

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world.

These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry's critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech).

Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.

But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.

On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead.

It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)

The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control.

But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China.

It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further.

What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.

But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good.

The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

#386. Teenage swimmer breaks two world records in four days

Sixteen-year-old Summer McIntosh broke the world record for the 400m individual medley at the Canadian swimming trials on Saturday – just days after breaking the world record for the 400m freestyle.

McIntosh finished the 400m individual medley in a time of 4:25.87, breaking the mark set at the 2016 Rio Olympics by Hungarian swimmer Katinka Hosszú with a time of 4:26.36.

The result continues the teenager’s brilliant week after she broke the 400m freestyle world record last Tuesday – breaking defending Olympic champion Ariarne Titmus’ previous record of 3:56.40, which was set last May, in a time of 3:56.08.

Speaking after her latest triumph, McIntosh shared her emotions.

“That’s the first time I really vividly heard the crowd during my race,” McIntosh said, per Reuters.

“It’s amazing to have all my family and friends in the stands, cheering me on. It really helped me in the last 100 meters.”

The Canadian teen made her Olympic debut aged 14 at Tokyo 2020, where she finished fourth in the 200-meter freestyle.

She bagged gold in the 200m butterfly and 400m medley at the world championships in 2022, as well as two golds at the Commonwealth Games in the 200m and 400m medleys.

She now trains in Florida under coach Brent Arckey with the Sarasota Sharks team.

#383. Sunrise on the Reaping review: The biggest and boldest Hunger Games yet

Are you looking for a movie to thoroughly wallop you? To leave you emotionally battered, physically exhausted, and full of despair and hope at the same time? Then allow me to prescribe a healthy dose of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, the sixth film in the Hunger Games series.

Based on Suzanne Collins' second prequel novel following The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, Sunrise on the Reaping once again rewinds the clock on Panem to the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell. These are the biggest Hunger Games yet, with 48 tributes instead of the standard 24. Among them is Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), future mentor to series protagonists Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark.

The question here is not whether Haymitch will survive the games. We know, by virtue of the entire original trilogy, that he does. But before he was the cynical, heavy-drinking, lone wolf victor audiences met in The Hunger Games, he was an optimistic 16-year-old with a caring family, a loving relationship, and a solid community in District 12. So the real question of Sunrise on the Reaping becomes, what broke that young man down so thoroughly? The answer is, unsurprisingly, bleak as all hell. But director Francis Lawrence executes it in thrilling (if occasionally overstuffed) fashion, with a Hunger Games sequence that blows series-high Catching Fire's own games out of the water, and a dogged focus on the philosophical themes at the core of Collins' work.

This being a Hunger Games movie, there are certain key beats it needs to hit. First, tributes need to be reaped. In this case, District 12's motley crew is made up of Haymitch, Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), and Louella McCoy (Molly McCann). From there, the tributes must go to the Capitol and witness its gaudy depravity for themselves. They get makeovers, train, give interviews, and eventually make their way into the Capitol's ultimate death trap.

Viewers have seen these beats before in The Hunger Games and Catching Fire. They also witnessed a deliberately scaled-back version in prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, which established the Games' evolution from what was essentially a run-down cage match to a glossy propaganda spectacle.

After sending us through three very different Hunger Games, how can the franchise create a new variation on the same brutal theme? First, by making Sunrise on the Reaping a heist movie. Granted, Haymitch and his allies aren't actually trying to steal anything from the Capitol. Rather, they're trying to break the arena and send a clear message. For that, Haymitch gets roped into a scheme cooked up by former victor Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) and his son, District 3 tribute Ampert (Percy Daggs IV). With a complex series of moving parts, Ampert and Haymitch's plan captures the essence of a dangerous heist, and Lawrence delivers the suspense to match.

Then, there's the arena. If you thought Catching Fire's clock was a sadistic marvel of game-making, not to mention a visual feast thanks to its tropical jungles and beaches, get ready for a level up. The arena for the Second Quarter Quell is a technicolor nightmare. Lush flower beds and crystal clear streams hide poisonous underbellies. Swarms of beautiful birds and butterflies will kill at a moment's notice. Even an idyllic, snow-capped mountain hides explosive horrors. Thankfully, Sunrise on the Reaping is actually colorful to match, its eye-popping hues reminding blockbuster filmmakers everywhere that yes, vibrancy is still possible!

That vibrancy in Sunrise on the Reaping extends to the broader world of Panem itself, which has taken on a distinctive '70s look. The Capitol is awash in glitzy psychedelics, a far cry from the post-war dilapidation of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. As the Games have grown more extravagant, so, too have the Capitol citizens. Take District 12 escort Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close, almost unrecognizable under prosthetics and an uncanny tape facelift). She is the pinnacle of excess, from her visible cosmetic work to her neon fashion. Close is chewing so much scenery she could probably devour the entire arena, but it's exactly what the role calls for: ridiculous pomp, circumstance, and venomous hatred for the Districts.

Drusilla is one of the new characters introduced in Sunrise on the Reaping. However, a big chunk of the film's supporting cast is made up of familiar figures from the original trilogy: Capitol insider Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons); master of ceremonies Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin); former victors Beetee, Mags (Lili Taylor), and Wiress (Maya Hawke); stylist Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning); and of course, President Coriolanus Snow (Ralph Fiennes). Their non-stop introductions give Sunrise on the Reaping an unfortunate case of prequel-itis, even if they play key roles in the story. Their presence also means the involvement of many new Capitol characters feels muted. Billy Porter's snake-loving stylist Magno Stift gets short shrift (and even shorter screen time), while his helpers Proserpina (Iris Apatow) and Vitus (Edvin Ryding) might as well be afterthoughts.

Thankfully, the District 12 newcomers fare far better. As Haymitch's great love Lenore Dove, Whitney Peak is a radiant beam of rebellious wisdom. Elsewhere, each of the tributes buck misconceptions about them to reveal their true mettle underneath. Maysilee may seem stuck-up and aloof at first, but Grace quickly unleashes the ferocious survivor in her. Wang brings kind courage to oddsmaker Wyatt, and McCann is steely sweet as Louella.

Leading it all is Zada, who does an admirable job making Haymitch his own, all while balancing Harrelson's mannerisms from the original trilogy. Put them saying "sweetheart" side by side and tell me that's not the same character, years apart.

Sunrise on the Reaping works hard to build out this captivating new version of Panem and the Games, but once it starts really playing in that sandbox, you're in for wave after wave of brutality. It's almost impressive how, after five books and six movies, the Hunger Games franchise can still find new ways to up the emotional pain of watching children fight to death under the thumb of an authoritarian regime. You'd think we'd already hit that peak with Rue's death in the first Hunger Games, and yet!

No spoilers, but let's just say I hope Zada's contract included a bonus for each time he had to cradle the body of a dear ally and tearfully beg them to stay with him. That his performance and the film never feel stale as they go through the motions of helpless grief time and time again is a testament to how distinct each of Haymitch's relationships feel.

But while Sunrise on the Reaping is arguably the Hunger Games at its most tragic, it's also the franchise at its angriest. Every instalment in the series has critiqued the Capitol, but Sunrise on the Reaping puts a laser focus on the mundane machinery that keeps these systems of power in place. As the film opens, we see Peacekeepers and Capitol staffers performing administrative tasks for the Reaping, like putting up barricades and placards dictating where children should stand. Elsewhere, the propaganda machine chugs along, with cameramen like Plutarch always finding the perfect shot to tell the Capitol's story. (And always knowing which context to leave out to make the Capitol look its absolute best.)

Throughout, though, Sunrise on the Reaping also turns its lens on Panem's citizens, asking why they allow themselves to be ruled by such a horrific regime. Collins opens Sunrise on the Reaping with several epigraphs, including two from Scottish philosopher David Hume, the first of which details his thoughts on implicit submission. The film takes that message to heart, repeatedly questioning what leads the many not to rise up against the few that govern them. Why do District 12's citizens stand mutely by while Drusilla and Plutarch re-stage a key moment from the Reaping ceremony? Why do armed tributes not turn on the unarmed Peacekeepers who oversee them at training? Sunrise on the Reaping doesn't take a subtle approach — at one point Plutarch straight-up says "no more implicit submission" — but then again, it's also vital to see a blockbuster not sand down the novel's overt messaging.

It's also vital for a film this heavy to have hope, and almost miraculously, Sunrise on the Reaping, does. The film emphasizes the fact of its title: that for Haymitch's whole life, the sun has always risen on the Reaping. But as Lenore tells him, just because that's the way things have been for so long doesn't mean they'll be that way forever. (Their conversation remixes the novel's second epigraph from Hume.)

Anyone who's watched or read the original Hunger Games series knows that Panem will one day see a world where the sun doesn't rise on the Reaping. It'll just take a lot of work and sacrifice to get there. In Sunrise on the Reaping, we get to witness the first sparks of that eventual reunion. Knowing where Haymitch's story ends turns his tragedy into a bittersweet bridge to the future, making Sunrise on the Reaping a perfect bookend to the Hunger Games franchise as it stands. (At least, until Collins decides to return to Panem.)

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping hits theaters Nov. 20.

#379. Shures new spatial audio mic was made with creators in mind

Spatial audio is having a moment in the creator-verse. Just last month, Sony introduced its ECM-AX10 spatial audio mic, and now Shure is entering the category with its USB-C MV360 and MV360+ spatial audio microphones.

"We know that more and more people — more and more creators — are kind of multidisciplinary, especially for folks who are maybe video first and then they have to worry about audio second," Steve Marek, Associate Product Manager at Shure, said in a briefing with Mashable. "So, we know that there's room for that industry to grow."

Marek said, "We really wanted to think of this as a microphone that people can grow with," and that rather than having five different audio recording tools, creators can do everything with the MV360 and have flexibility with their audio output.

The MV360 retails for $349 and is available now. The microphone kit comes with the USB-C mic, a tripod, a cold shoe mic clip, a 5/8-inch mic clip, a phone clamp, two USB-C cables, a carrying case, and a foam windscreen. The microphone also has an onboard 3.5mm headphone jack.

The MV360 features four capture modes: mono, stereo, immersive binaural, and auto tracking. The latter uses virtual microphones that steer toward the loudest sound source and is ideal for recording podcasts, interviews, or moving subjects. Regardless of capture mode, you'll get a ready-to-use two-channel audio file that requires no post-production work — though it is compatible with editing apps and devices should you want to adjust or edit.

The MV360 can be as simple or as complex as you want. If you're a skilled audio engineer, you can mix to your heart's desire. Or if you've never seen audio software in your life, you have perfectly good sound straight from the mic.

The MV360+ is not available yet, but will be the more advanced option geared toward field recordists, videographers, and VR storytellers. It'll pair with DSLR cameras, action cameras, and 360 cameras. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Shure's MOTIV app is where you can set your capture mode and edit audio that you've recorded. There are plenty of presets and adjustable settings that you can play around with, too. Slide the level adjuster to capture every minor sound for ASMR or to avoid audio spiking. You can even select where the microphone is oriented in relation to the subject — whether it's facing up, down, or on its side. There's a little diagram in the app that shows a sound heat map, so you can see exactly from which direction sound is hitting the microphone.

You can record and edit directly in the app. And one really cool feature is that you can move "virtual microphones" after you've already recorded to better boost directional sound.

I received a test unit of the MV360 microphone ahead of its launch and have had a chance to play around with it a bit. It sounds great for unboxing videos — it picks up on all the crispy sounds without sounding blown out. I tested some whispering ASMR, and I was able to boost the audio levels in the companion app before recording to really pick up on every minor sound. I will be using this as an excuse to buy a bunch of weird candy from Five Below to further test the microphone's ASMR-ability, so stay tuned for that. We'll have a full review of the MV360 coming later.

My only minor frustration with the microphone is how bulky/heavy it is. With pocket mics, like the DJI Mic Mini, there's a small receiver that you plug into your phone. The MV360 plugs directly into your phone or computer via USB-C, so it's tethered to your recording device. Clamping my phone and the mic to the tripod was just a little clunky when oriented in portrait mode. But its heft also makes sense, considering how much more advanced the audio recording is compared to small creator mics.

Also, I love that Shure includes a tripod with the MV360, but I found myself reaching for my personal tripod for most of my recordings.

Neither of those are reason enough to discredit the microphone at all — just some minor learning curves.

The MV360 is available now from Shure and third-party retailers like Amazon for $349. The MV360+ will be available in early 2027 for $449.

The gesture has sparked much debate, especially on social media. Some have criticized Reese, while others have defended her actions, highlighting how there was no public outrage in response to Clark’s gesture earlier in the tournament.

Sports journalist Jose de Jesus Ortiz called Reese’s actions “classless,” while former ESPN host Keith Olbermann called Reese an “idiot” for the gesture.

In the press conference after the victory, Reese referenced the difference in reaction she received as a result of her gesture as compared to the one Clark received.

“All year, I was critiqued for who I was. I don’t fit the narrative,” Reese said. “I don’t fit the box that y’all want me to be in. I’m too hood. I’m too ghetto. Y’all told me that all year. But when other people do it, and y’all don’t say nothing.

“So this is for the girls that look like me. For those that want to speak up for what they believe in. It’s unapologetically you. And that’s what I did it for tonight. It was bigger than me tonight. And Twitter is going to go into a rage every time.

“And I’m happy. I feel like I’ve helped grow women’s basketball this year. (…) I’m looking forward to celebrating and then next season.”

LSU beats Iowa to win its first NCAA women's basketball championship

Reese had 15 points and 10 rebounds in the 102-85 victory and won the women’s March Madness’ Most Outstanding Player award.

In the post-game broadcast, Reese referenced the similar gesture Clark made to a Louisville opponent in the Elite Eight.

In the same game, Clark said to an opponent: “You’re down by 15 points. Shut up,” according to the Bleacher Report.

“Caitlin Clark is a hell of a player but I don’t take disrespect lightly,” Reese said. “She disrespected [LSU’s] Alexis [Morris] (…) and I wanted to pick her pocket. But I had a moment at the end of her game. I was in my bag, I was in my moment.”

After the Championship game, Clark herself said she didn’t notice anything at the time.

“I was just trying to get to the handshake line and shake hands and be grateful that my team was in that position,” Clark said in the post-game press conference. “All the credit in the world to LSU. They were tremendous. They deserve it. They had a tremendous season.

“(LSU head coach) Kim Mulkey coached them so, so well. She’s one of the best basketball coaches of all time, and it shows. She only said really kind things to me in the handshake line, so I’m very grateful of that too.

“But honestly I have no idea. I was just trying to spend the last few moments on the court with especially the five people that I’ve started 93 games with and relishing every second of that.”

LSU head coach Mulkey said she had “no clue” about what transpired.

Among those defending Reese on social media were ESPN’s Holly Rowe and former NBA star Etan Thomas.

“People hating on Angel Reese or Caitlin Clark. Stop. Unapologetically confident young women should be celebrated NOT hated. Get used to it,” Rowe wrote on Twitter.

Former Washington Wizards, Oklahoma City Thunder and Atlanta Hawks player Thomas wrote: “Hold on now!!!! It was cute when Caitlin Clark did it. Y’all didn’t have any issues with it at all. So don’t be all outraged and talking about class and sportsmanship when Angel Reese does the same thing. We’re not doing double standards here.”

Reese said the negative reaction on social media throughout the season has helped fuel her excellent season, having finished averaging 23.0 points and 15.4 rebounds in her first season with LSU after transferring from Maryland.

“Twitter can say what they want to say,” she said. “I love reading those comments. I have all the screenshots of what everybody has said about me all season. What are you going to say now?”

Regional and Shiny encounters in Pokémon GO: Finishing seven days of lessons generates a unique offer code redeemable on the Pokémon GO Web Store. That unlocks Timed Research featuring XP, Stardust, and guaranteed encounters with Pikachu, Meowth, Lucario, and regional-exclusive Chatot.

Foreign-language gameplay and new language tags: When you activate the Timed Research, you pick a target language, and your tasks actually appear in that language. #375. Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer

Drought conditions and low reservoir levels are affecting the renewable power source.

The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source.

Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River. And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.

Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September.

Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.

Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.

The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.

But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study. Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.

Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA.

El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions.

Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

These scientists hope that fire-spotting satellites, AI tools and ancient land practices could preserve the world’s vulnerable permafrost—and the vast carbon it stores.

New technology could help cut power losses and reinvent a staple of the grid.

Batteries that swap liquid electrolytes for solid materials promise to charge faster, last longer, and (crucially) run cooler.

#373. Xiaomi 18 Pro hands-on: Undeniably cool, incredibly powerful

What if your phone had a second display on the back?

If you've asked yourself this question, or have peered lustfully at the new foldable phones, including from Apple, you should take a look at the new Xiaomi 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max. The display is very cool and does bring some functionality that you otherwise just cannot have, though it's not nearly as versatile as what you get with a foldable phone.

I've spent a few days with both phones, and I can tell you, these are incredibly fast, capable, and sleek devices, albeit a little iPhone-like. The display on the back is what makes them stand out from the crowd, at least visually, but it's not something that will drastically change the way you use your phone.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro series is not Xiaomi's first phone to feature a secondary display on the back; last year's Xiaomi 17 Pro had one, too. Just like the main display on the front, it hasn't changed much since last year: It's still a 2.9-inch, 596x976 pixel AMOLED display, though it is a little brighter than before. I didn't get to try the 17 Pro, though, so the display on the back is new to me.

Displays: 6.9-inch, 1,208x2,624 pixel, 120Hz AMOLED display with 4000 nits of peak brightness; secondary display on the back: 2.9-inch, 120Hz AMOLED display with 4000 nits of peak brightness

Design: Dragon Crystal Glass 3 front, aluminum frame,

Size and weight: 163.4 x 77.6 x 8.4 mm; weight: 240 grams

Rear cameras: A triple rear camera system with a 200-megapixel, f/1.7 wide camera, a 200-megapixel, f/2.4 periscope telephoto camera, and a 50-megapixel, f/2.4 ultrawide camera

Front cameras: 50-megapixel, f/2.2 selfie camera

Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6.

Storage: 256GB/512GB/1TB with 12/16GB of RAM

Battery life: 7,050mAh battery with 100W charging, 50 wireless, and 27W reverse wireless charging

Special features: Under display ultrasonic fingerprint scanner, stereo audio system with 3 speakers, 24-bit/192kHz hi-res audio support

Yes, this is an extremely powerful phone, even though it isn't technically Xiaomi's flagship (that's the Ultra series, which isn't out yet this year). You get the latest Snapdragon chip, a massive camera upgrade over last year's 50-megapixel system, and a humongous battery that charges very quickly.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro, which I also received for testing but have spent less time with, has a 6.4-inch display, a smaller battery, with the rest being mostly the same.

Xiaomi flagships in the numbered series follow the same philosophy: Make a phone that's very much like an iPhone, but stuff it with extremely powerful hardware for added value. It starts with the phones' names (18 Pro and 18 Pro Max), it's visible in parts of the design, and Xiaomi's HyperOS, which has been upgraded to version 4 here, can be set up to mirror iOS in almost every way.

This is not a bad thing. The Xiaomi 18 Pro is distinctive enough with its dual display that overall iPhone-likeness doesn't feel like you're having a cheap copy. And I don't mind the HyperOS software being a dead ringer for iOS, down to the near-identical Control Center (which, you guessed it, is called the Control Center on the Xiaomi as well).

Do I need a display on the back of the phone? Not really. It's useful for photos as it can give cues to the folks you're photographing, and it can take your selfies game to the next level as you can actually take selfies with the 200-megapixel main camera system. Other than that, it just looks cool.

But you do need to see it in real life to appreciate just how cool it is. It's an excellent, super-bright, pixel-dense AMOLED display with a 120Hz refresh rate. I set it up with an ocean wave animation that looks downright beautiful when I touch it. You can have AI-based apps on there, and even use it for simple games. It's so good that I kept consciously placing the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max on its face when setting it on a table, just to appreciate the crispness of that mini display on the back.

But other than the camera tricks, it's still (surprise!) preferable to use the much larger front display for most tasks. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Up until a few years ago, battery capacities north of 5,000mAh were reserved for thick specialty phones focusing on battery life. But then a couple of battery breakthroughs (including silicon-carbon battery tech which Xiaomi is using here) made it to the mass market, and now Xiaomi can place an 7,050mAh battery in the regular-sized Xiaomi 18 Pro Max.

The battery charges quickly on a fast charger and it lasts for at least two days. It's so good that I didn't have proper time to really test it as I only charged the phone twice in little under a week.

I don't think I've ever used a Xiaomi phone that was as quick and worked as smoothly as this one. Everything I touched opened instantly (including the fingerprint scanner which takes a tiny fraction of a second to analyze your digit and log you in). Playing with animated, AI-based and fancy perspective wallpapers did not punish me in terms of speed, as the phone kept operating incredibly smoothly.

Yes, it has the latest Snapdragon chip inside, but I guess Xiaomi also polished its HyperOS 4 to make it a little speedier than before.

As is customary for Xiaomi, HyperOS does have a maddening number of features and options, some of which are tucked away in some menu you wouldn't think of. But given the versatility of this phone, it's hard to blame them. One I set the phone up as I liked, the complexity of the Settings did not bother me.

We've gotten to a point in which Xiaomi can put two 200-megapixel cameras, and a two 50-megapixel ones on a phone that's not really their camera flagship.

Do we need so many megapixels? Possibly not, as evidenced in the fact that Xiaomi 18 Pro Max takes 12.5 megapixel photos by default, and you have to manually up the resolution to either 50 or 200 megapixels.

But the high megapixel count opens up interesting possibilities, such as zooming in at 12.8x without losing quality. The telephoto camera doubles as a macro camera that can go in really close (its minimum focusing distance is 12 centimetres), with Xiaomi calling it a "telescope and microscope in one."

I haven't had enough time with the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's camera to fully assess how good it is. From what I've seen, though, it's an incredibly versatile and powerful system that you can use to squeeze out a good photo in almost every scenario.

#369. We found 14 early Black Friday Apple deals: Score AirPods and MacBooks on sale

Apple raised its prices this year, but who didn't? Well, now that Black Friday sale season is here, this is your best chance to cancel out those price hikes. That's why we're paying extra close attention to early Black Friday Apple deals.

Yes, Apple does do Black Friday, but not in the way you might expect. Shopping directly on Apple's website usually means getting a measly gift card for future purchases. The real way to find great deals? Looking at retailers like Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, and Target. Especially as Black Friday approaches (mark Nov. 27 in your calendar), retailers duke it out to see who can offer the best prices on AirPods, MacBooks, and iPads. Walmart and Amazon are infamous for outdoing each other by a single cent.

Usually, prices on Apple products drop to record lows during the hectic Black Friday weekend. However, especially good deals can also sell out quick. In my five years covering Black Friday at Mashable, I've seen many an AirPod Pro deal go out of stock before I could finish writing a 200-word story about the deal.

Shopping early lets you score decent savings while avoiding the post-Thanksgiving chaos. So, how do you know what to buy, and what to save for Black Friday and Cyber Monday? That's where the expertise of the Mashable shopping team can be helpful.

Let's start with the very expensive elephant in the room. In June, Apple raised prices on MacBooks, Macs, iPads, the HomePod, Apple TVs, and even the Vision Pro headset, followed by iPhone price increases in September. With many products rising to $200 or more, the likelihood of seeing them fall to record-low prices is, well, low. Instead, I research the market to identify products at or near record lows over the past five months.

I also took into account the frequency of deals. If, like the AirPods Pro 3, there's a $50 deal that's nearly always on, I don't necessarily consider that a deal worth highlighting. On the other hand, if an iPad is $100 off for the first time in a month, I'll include it and note its pricing history.

Finally, I considered our reviewers' first-hand experiences with these products. Most of the items in this guide have been hands-on tested by at least one person on the Mashable staff, and I prioritized Mashable award winners, choosing the best deals based on overall product performance and value. #368. Grindr launches $120/month subscription with AI chat summaries

After testing a rumored $499/month subscription tier, gay hookup app Grindr is officially launching Edge, an AI-focused plan running for $120 a month in the U.S. or $70 per week.

Edge has three main features: Insights, which shows users compatibility and likelihood to reply; Recommendations, which provides five curated profiles a day; and Reconnect (called A-List in beta), which highlights past connections and generates summaries of your conversations.

Edge includes everything that's in Grindr's Unlimited subscription, as well, which includes features like being able to scroll through unlimited profiles, incognito mode, unsending messages, and expiring photos.

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups

Pure — best for anonymous hookups

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity

Edge is powered by Grindr's proprietary AI stack called "gAI." Users can control which sensitive data to provide gAI and whether the app can use this to develop gAI over time. Such data can include preferred position, ethnicity, and user chats.

Grindr states that certain health data won't be used in gAI, like HIV status, last tested date, testing reminders, the "Poz" tribe and tag (which stands for the HIV-positive community), and vaccination status. Grindr recently settled a lawsuit for £26 million after allegedly sharing users' HIV statuses with third parties. (Grindr denied the allegations.) Shortly after, the app acquired a provider of the HIV-prevention medication PrEP, and plans to provide PrEP on the app.

Mashable received an early demo of Edge last week, during which Grindr's chief product officer, AJ Balance, said that Edge is the app's most personalized experience yet.

Balance said that Grindr users are at the forefront of culture and tech, and the Grindr team believes it's their job to leverage new technology. As AI was unfolding and it was clear it was the next paradigm shift, Grindr saw an opportunity to utilize it to add value to its users' lives.

Enthusiasm for Edge was apparently high during beta testing, Balance told Mashable, and beta testers ultimately want more connection with less effort and reduced friction in finding a match. The blog post Balance penned for the release is even called, "More Action, Less Effort."

What about the alleged $499/month price tag for the subscription?

Balance said that the app tested a range of pricing. And while $120 is much less than $499, Grindr CEO George Arison defended the price to BBC News today, saying that, "I think we're a capitalist society, and everything hinges on whether you can afford it or not." Balance told Mashable that 91 percent of its users use the app for free, while the remaining 9 percent are power users who want more convenience and ease to save time.

Edge is now available globally to all Grindr users on iOS and Android.

#367. ‘The Predators Are Real’: Senate Hearing Slams Roblox Over Child Sex Abuse

People who say they were groomed on Roblox testified in front of a Congressional subcommittee Tuesday about safety risks associated with the popular gaming platform frequented by kids and teenagers.

“Roblox is one of the most popular gaming platforms in the world,” Republican senator Josh Hawley said in his opening remarks. “If your children are on Roblox they are being exposed in all likelihood to sexual predators … to sexually exploitative content, left, right, and center.”

The hearing was intended to address the bipartisan legislation introduced by Hawley and Democratic senator Dick Durbin, coauthors of the No Forced Arbitration for Child Sexual Exploitation and Cyber Injuries Act, which would allow families of victims to sue Roblox directly instead of being forced to settle their claims privately in arbitration, as the platform’s terms of service currently dictate.

The process of forced arbitration “strips consumers and workers of their rights,” testified Myriam Gilles, a law professor at Northwestern University who is an expert on forced arbitration. “I never expected to come before this body to talk about its use against 9-year-olds, but that’s where we are.”

Roblox is currently facing nearly 200 lawsuits from families who allege that their children were groomed by sexual predators posing as children on the platform. According to Hawley, Roblox CEO David Baszucki was invited to testify at the hearing but declined.

“He may think he’s silent, but in fact he’s testifying, and what he’s testifying to is his commitment to money over people,” Hawley said.

In a statement, Sara Kanawati Stephany, a senior manager for US policy communications at Roblox, told WIRED, “Safety has been central to Roblox since we launched. We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat. A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety. Protecting children online takes stronger protections, better tools, and consistent standards that apply everywhere kids spend time online.”

Roblox has previously argued that users waive their right to sue in open court in the platform’s terms of agreement. According to Roblox’s own data, 35 percent of its age-checked daily active users are under the age of 13—too young to fully comprehend the terms of the agreement, witnesses argued.

“There is no way an 8-year-old could read those terms and then sign away their right to a moment in court, effectively silencing themselves,” Republican senator Katie Britt said after being presented with a copy of the multi-page agreement.

Two of those who testified before Congress were alleged survivors of grooming on the platform. One was Michael Schlep, a content creator who has advocated for more stringent child safety measures on the platform.

Schlep testified that when he was 12, he met a game developer on the platform who befriended him in a public chatroom, then moved to private chats. He alleges he was exposed to “violent pornography, cartel beheadings, and extreme racist ideologies” that he says was a result of his communication with this adult man, and that his abuser exposed his private information, leading to a suicide attempt. He currently runs a YouTube channel exposing alleged Roblox child predators and criticizing the platform for failing to protect children, which has led to Roblox hitting him with a cease-and-desist.

“Roblox must be held accountable publicly,” Schlep testified. “They will not voluntarily act to protect children.”

The hearing also featured testimony from a Marine Corps veteran identified as Woody Doe, who alleged that he was groomed, then sexually assaulted by an adult man he met on Roblox when he was 11 years old. “For years, I carried the shame of what happened,” he testified. He now has a lawsuit pending against Roblox for allegedly failing to warn parents and children of the dangers of the platform.

“I cannot go back and protect the 11-year-old boy I once was, but I can speak for him today … and prevent any other children from ever experiencing the same pain,” he said.

Roblox is a massive gaming platform, with about 138 million daily active users according to recent company data. As of 2025, 39.7 million daily active users were under the age of 13.

In response to the litigation and to intense media scrutiny, Roblox has adopted what it says are more stringent child-safety measures, including AI-assisted face recognition to estimate a user’s age. But Khari James, senior legal counsel at the National Center on Sexual Exploitation said face-recognition technology isn’t always accurate, and predators could potentially purchase verified accounts to continue to prey on children. Doing face verifications just once, she argues, gives predators “complete access to all the children on Roblox.”

“Roblox may be a virtual world, but the children are real,” James said during her testimony. “The predators are real. The addiction is real. The exploitation is real, and the consequences are real. Children should never have to enter a game marketed to them and wonder whether the person on the other side of the screen is there to play with them or prey on them.”

#366. Supreme Court keeps injunction against DEI grant defunding in place

Appeals court ruling rejected grant cancellations on First Amendment grounds.

On Monday, the Supreme Court announced it would not hear an appeal of a lower court decision that blocked the government from canceling the grants of a handful of researchers whose funding had been revoked during the Trump administration’s purge of DEI-related work. While the decision applies to only seven researchers in California, the lower court had ruled that the government’s actions violated the First Amendment and so may have broad implications.

The Supreme Court provided no discussion of its rejection, and no justices filed a dissent regarding the decision.

The suit was initially filed by a large group of researchers at the University of California, Berkeley and UC San Francisco, contesting grants originally issued by many federal agencies, from the National Institutes of Health to the Department of Transportation. At issue were grants that had been terminated because the agencies decided they violated a Trump executive order blocking the use of DEI. This occurred despite the fact that the government hadn’t bothered to define DEI, and targeted grants were often identified by little more than a keyword search.

In the wake of a Supreme Court decision that held that most grant termination cases had to be heard by a different court, the case was narrowed considerably to just seven UC researchers and a handful of agencies: The Environmental Protection Agency, the National Science Foundation, and the National Endowment for the Humanities.

The researchers argued that the grant cancellations were viewpoint discrimination that violated the First Amendment. A District Court agreed, issuing a preliminary injunction that would restore the grants given to these researchers.

That decision was upheld by a Court of Appeals panel. It ruled that, while the government has the option of eliminating grant programs that it determined were no longer appropriate, canceling individual grants that it disagreed with is an attempt at “suppression of dangerous ideas.” In support of this, it cited Supreme Court precedent regarding religious viewpoint discrimination.

The court ruled that DEI fits in this framework because it “convey[s] the viewpoint that the exclusion of historically disadvantaged groups is undesirable.” As a result, “the government has not merely exercised its power to choose the programs it funds but has instead terminated individual grants in existing programs based on the perceived viewpoints of individual speakers.”

Assuming this case continues, the Supreme Court may find other chances to intervene. But the fact that it hasn’t done so now is striking, given that it could easily have objected to everything from the venue to the decision that the government’s actions constituted viewpoint discrimination. And its lack of intervention may be interpreted by other courts as a sign that the government’s anti-DEI efforts are on shaky legal ground.
